title: Singleton Pattern
oneLiner: Guarantees a class has exactly one instance and gives the whole app a single point of access to it.

hero.name: The One
hero.catchphrase: There can only be one of me. Ask, and I shall appear — always the same.
hero.power: Guarantees a single, shared instance exists no matter how many times it's requested.
hero.weakness: Overused, The One becomes a hidden dependency that's hard to test and secretly couples every part of the app together.
hero.origin: Forged in a codebase where five different database connections were opened for the same database, The One swore that never again would duplicate state cause chaos.

story.problem: A configuration object gets created every time it's needed. Three different parts of the app each construct their own copy, read stale settings, and silently drift out of sync.
story.solution: The One steps in: the class controls its own construction, hands out the same instance every time, and refuses to ever be built twice.
story.result: Every corner of the app now shares one consistent source of truth, with no duplicate state and no drift.

before: Multiple copies of config drift out of sync
Wasted memory and setup cost on every construction
No single source of truth to debug against
after: A single, well-known place to inspect state

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Config is being constructed in three different places. Nobody agrees on the settings anymore.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Wait — why does the logger think debug mode is off, but the API client thinks it's on?!

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: A glowing seal appears around the Config class. The One has arrived.
panels.speaker: The One
panels.dialogue: You don't need a new instance. You need THE instance. Let me handle that.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: The constructor is sealed. A private static instance is born, and a public gateway hands it out on request.
panels.speaker: The One
panels.dialogue: Call getInstance() as many times as you like. You will always receive me — the same me.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: One config. One truth. Every module reads the exact same settings, instantly in sync.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Debug mode finally agrees with itself. I could cry.

useWhen: Exactly one instance must coordinate actions across the whole app (e.g. a connection pool, a config store, a logging pipeline).
Creating the object is expensive and reuse clearly saves work.
You need a well-known access point that many unrelated modules can reach without passing it through every layer.
avoidWhen: You're using it as a shortcut to avoid passing dependencies explicitly — that just hides coupling instead of removing it.
The 'single instance' assumption might not hold in the future (multi-tenant apps, multiple config profiles, parallel test runs).
It would need to hold mutable state read and written from many places — that's a recipe for hidden bugs.
commonMistakes: Turning ordinary shared services into Singletons just because they're used 'everywhere' — most of the time a single instance passed via dependency injection is enough, and stays testable.
Forgetting that global state makes unit tests order-dependent, since one test's mutation leaks into the next.
Not handling concurrent initialization correctly in multi-threaded environments, causing two instances to be created briefly.
Using a Singleton to fake global variables instead of solving the actual architectural problem.
explanation.realWorldExample: Database connection pools, application-wide loggers, and the browser's `window` object are all effectively Singletons — one shared instance the whole runtime talks to.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So The One just... stops you from making more than one instance?

conversation.speaker: The One
conversation.message: Exactly. The constructor is private. The only door in is getInstance() — and I already know who's home.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't that just a fancy global variable?

conversation.speaker: The One
conversation.message: If you overuse me, yes — and that's my weakness. Used sparingly, for things that truly must be singular, I keep your app consistent instead of tangled.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app opens a new database connection pool every time a request handler runs, exhausting the database's max-connections limit within minutes of going live.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The One guarantees the connection pool is created exactly once and reused everywhere, so you never exceed the database's connection limit.

quiz.question: What is the core guarantee a Singleton provides?
options: Only one instance of the class ever exists, and everyone shares it
The class can be instantiated only from a factory
Every property on the class is read-only
The class automatically saves itself to a database
quiz.answer: Only one instance of the class ever exists, and everyone shares it
quiz.explanation: That single shared instance, reachable from anywhere, is the entire point of the pattern.

quiz.question: How does a typical Singleton implementation prevent extra instances from being created?
options: By making the constructor private and exposing a static getInstance() method
By throwing an error every time 'new' is used anywhere in the file
By deleting the class after first use
By storing the instance in a global array and picking one at random
quiz.answer: By making the constructor private and exposing a static getInstance() method
quiz.explanation: Sealing the constructor forces all callers through the single controlled access point.

quiz.question: What's the biggest risk of overusing the Singleton pattern?
options: It creates hidden global state that couples unrelated parts of the app and complicates testing
It makes the application slower on every single method call
It prevents the app from ever being deployed to more than one server
It requires a database to function
quiz.answer: It creates hidden global state that couples unrelated parts of the app and complicates testing
quiz.explanation: Because a Singleton is reachable from anywhere, it's easy for it to become an untracked dependency, making code harder to reason about and to test in isolation.

quiz.question: You need a class that will eventually support multiple named configuration profiles (e.g. per-tenant settings). Is Singleton the right call?
options: No — Singleton assumes exactly one instance forever, which conflicts with needing several distinct instances
Yes — Singleton can easily be reconfigured later to support multiple instances
Yes — Singleton is required whenever configuration is involved
No — Singleton can only be used for logging
quiz.answer: No — Singleton assumes exactly one instance forever, which conflicts with needing several distinct instances
quiz.explanation: If you anticipate needing more than one instance, avoid locking yourself into 'exactly one' — use a registry or dependency injection instead.
